topStories.headline: Heber City Renews IT Contract as October Cyberattack Investigation Continues
topStories.dek: The City Council unanimously voted to extend its deal with Executech for $174,000 a year while the FBI's forensic probe of an October breach remains open.
topStories.body:
At its November 17 meeting, the Heber City Council unanimously approved a one-year contract renewal with Executech, a Utah-based cybersecurity firm, at $14,500 per month — $174,000 annually. The city has worked with Executech for more than a decade, and city Public Information Officer Ryan Bunnell said the arrangement may be more cost-effective than hiring a dedicated full-time IT employee depending on workload.

The renewal comes as Heber City continues to investigate a cyberattack that breached its municipal IT network on October 10. The city's separately hosted website was not affected, and officials have said residents can use online bill pay and other services at heberut.gov with confidence. Police Department records were also stored separately and were not compromised.

The FBI is assisting with a forensic investigation. Bunnell said in a written statement to the Park Record that the city will disclose whether any truly sensitive information — such as personal data — was accessed once the full picture becomes clear. 'Thank you for your patience as Heber City, assisted by Executech, sifts through the data and cleans up the mess that this threat actor inflicted upon us,' Bunnell said.

topStories.headline: Newly Elected Wasatch County Councilmembers Put Brakes on Dense Development
topStories.dek: Republicans Rachel Kahler, Erik Rowland, and Michael Murphy won all three contested council seats in the November 3 election and say limiting dense growth is a top priority.
topStories.body:
With 64 percent voter turnout and more than 14,000 ballots cast, Wasatch County elected three Republicans to its council in the November 3 general election. Rachel Kahler took Seat A — a countywide seat — while Erik Rowland and Michael Murphy won their respective districts. All three candidates have signaled that curbing high-density residential development will be among their first priorities when they take office.

Kahler, the executive director of Community Alliance for Main Street and a former Heber City councilmember, said her focus will be ensuring the county is adequately prepared for growth, including having the right water and waste management systems in place. She specifically said she will oppose high-density projects pursued through SB258, the 2024 preliminary municipality law that the Wasatch and Summit county councils have both called on the Legislature to repeal.

Murphy, whose district includes Hideout, Timber Lakes, and eastern Wasatch County, also listed limiting dense development as a priority. The results cement Republican control of the council heading into 2027, a year that will bring significant land-use decisions as the valley continues to attract interest from developers.

topStories.headline: Wasatch County's Proposed 2027 Budget Holds the Line — No Tax Increase
topStories.dek: County leaders reviewed a $130.8 million tentative budget on November 18 that keeps the property tax rate flat while adding six new staff positions.
topStories.body:
The Wasatch County Council reviewed its tentative 2027 budget at a November 18 meeting, and the bottom line is essentially unchanged from 2026: the proposed budget of $130.8 million is about $66,000 less than the current year's $130.9 million figure. Crucially, the draft does not include a property tax rate increase. Any additional property tax revenue in the budget comes from new growth, not a higher rate.

The general fund, at $55.2 million, is up from $52.4 million in 2026. It includes six new positions, among them a code enforcement role in the county attorney's office. Assistant County Manager Heber Lefgren said changes to the county's IT department structure would reduce internal service fees charged to other departments, and the county also plans to extend the useful life of certain fleet vehicles from five years to seven.

Council members continued to debate potential additional spending cuts, with at least one councilmember questioning whether residents' financial pressures would justify cuts large enough to reduce services. Additional budget discussions are planned throughout the rest of November before a final vote.

moreNews.headline: Après Dermatology Opens Second Location in Heber City
moreNews.body: The Heber Valley Chamber of Commerce held a ribbon-cutting ceremony this week for Après Dermatology and Cosmetic Center's new Heber City location, the practice's second office after its established Park City clinic. The practice is owned and operated by Dr. Timothy C. Michaelis, MD, FAAD. The clinic is currently accepting new patients and most insurance for both dermatological and cosmetic services.

moreNews.headline: Christian Center Distributes Free Turkeys at Heber Valley Pantry Ahead of Thanksgiving
moreNews.body: On Thursday, November 19, the Christian Center of Park City distributed free turkeys at its Heber Valley Food Pantry at 55 East Center Street — part of an 1,800-turkey giveaway funded by the Park City Board of Realtors Philanthropic Foundation. The distribution follows the closure earlier this fall of the Community Action Services and Food Bank pantry in Heber City, which had served roughly 60 families a week for more than eight years. The Christian Center has responded by increasing client visits at its Heber location from two to three times per month. Holiday meal bag donations are being collected through December at drop-off bins located at Wasatch High School, Heber Valley Hospital, the Heber City Administration Building, Midway City offices, and other locations.

moreNews.headline: Winter Parking Restrictions Now in Effect on Heber City and County Roads
moreNews.body: As of November 15, Heber City's winter parking ban is in effect: no vehicles may be parked on the paved portion of city streets or within five feet of pavement under City Code 10.16.040. The rule runs through April 1. Wasatch County adopted a parallel seasonal ordinance prohibiting parking on paved county roads between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m., and whenever snow is falling, is on the ground, or roads have not yet been plowed. Both rules are aimed at keeping roads clear for snow-removal crews during storms.
